posts.name: Timothy Chinecherem
posts.cooked:
Hi everyone,

I’ve been testing a recovery problem around CKB light-client wallets.

When you restore a wallet with your seed phrase, you get control of your wallet again.

But the wallet may still have to rebuild a lot of the local information it had already gathered before — account discovery, transaction history, live Cells, sync progress, light-client state, and other data it needs to become fully useful again.

I wanted to see if that part could also be recovered safely.

That became Waymark.

GitHub:

github.com

GitHub - Ticoworld/waymark

Contribute to Ticoworld/waymark development by creating an account on GitHub.

The idea

Waymark separates two things that normally get treated as one recovery problem:

1. Recovering ownership of the wallet

This still happens normally with the seed phrase.

The new installation creates its own keys, PIN protection, device security and signing environment.

2. Recovering useful local state

Before the old installation is lost, selected non-secret wallet and light-client state can be saved.

After the wallet is recovered normally on the new installation, that saved state can be restored too.

The wallet then continues syncing from there and checks everything against the chain.

So the flow looks like this:

Restore wallet normally
        ↓
keys and signing access are recovered
        ↓
restore saved non-secret wallet/light-client state
        ↓
continue syncing from that point
        ↓
catch up with anything that changed
        ↓
current chain state remains the final authority

The saved state is not treated as truth forever.

It can be old.

Cells that were live when it was saved may already have been spent. New transactions may have happened. Balances may have changed.

The wallet still has to reconnect to the chain and catch up correctly.

The point is simply that it does not always need to throw away all the useful work it had already done and start rebuilding everything from zero.

What is saved

The tested package contains selected non-secret information needed to continue the wallet’s previous work.

That includes things around:

  • public account relationships;
  • account and Script mapping;
  • sync progress;
  • discovery state;
  • light-client history and indexes;
  • chain checkpoints needed to continue syncing.

It does not contain the wallet’s signing secrets.

Waymark does not transfer:

  • seed phrase;
  • private keys;
  • wallet PIN;
  • Android device credential;
  • Android Keystore keys;
  • source-device signing material;
  • raw wallet backups containing secrets.

The wallet still has to be recovered normally first.

That was an important part of the test.

Why I tested it on Pocket Node

Pocket Node was a good place to test this because it runs a CKB light client directly on the device and keeps useful local state around the wallet.

I tested against Pocket Node 1.8.5.

Pocket itself was not modified into a finished Waymark feature.

The recovery/export/import work was done around the existing Pocket implementation so I could test whether the recovery model actually works.

How I tested it

I did not only test restoring a clean snapshot and checking whether the app opened.

The saved state was intentionally allowed to become stale.

After the checkpoint was created, more activity happened on the wallet.

That meant the restored wallet had to prove that it could continue from the older state and still discover what changed afterwards.

The later tests included:

  • two populated accounts;
  • different CKB Scripts;
  • transaction history on both accounts;
  • an active Nervos DAO deposit;
  • transactions that happened after the saved checkpoint;
  • account mapping checks;
  • balance and live Cell checks;
  • signing;
  • restart;
  • and comparison against the expected chain state.

After the emulator tests passed, I ran the full recovery flow on a real Android phone.

The final comparison

I tested two separate recovery paths.

Baseline recovery

For the baseline, Pocket started from fresh application state.

The wallet was recovered normally from the seed.

No saved Waymark state was used.

Pocket had to rebuild the required wallet/light-client state normally.

After recovery it reached the expected chain state, signed a real CKB testnet transaction, broadcast it successfully and passed a cold restart.

State-assisted recovery

Then Pocket was reset again.

The same wallet was recovered normally from the seed first.

This created fresh destination-side security again.

Only after normal recovery was complete did I restore the older saved non-secret state.

That saved checkpoint was stale by this point.

There had already been later activity on both accounts, including the transaction created during the baseline recovery.

So the restored wallet still had work to do.

It had to:

  • catch up from the saved checkpoint;
  • discover the later transactions;
  • remove Cells that were no longer live;
  • find the new live Cells;
  • recover the correct balances;
  • keep both accounts mapped correctly;
  • recover the DAO position correctly;
  • and reach the same current wallet state as the baseline recovery.

It passed.

After catching up, the state-assisted recovery also signed and confirmed another real testnet transaction.

It then passed a cold restart as well.

Result

At the common comparison point, baseline recovery and state-assisted recovery matched.

They agreed on:

  • both accounts;
  • account-to-Script mapping;
  • live Cells;
  • balances;
  • covered transaction history;
  • later activity that happened after the saved checkpoint;
  • DAO ownership and deposit state;
  • and sync progress.

There was no recovery-specific DAO difference.

There was no account mix-up.

There was no dependency on the old device’s Keystore.

The destination created its own fresh security state and signing still worked after the saved state was restored.

So for the Pocket setup I tested, the result was:

PASS

The baseline test transaction was:

0x2067edf16ab143e7bff9ef91803e36ce6a32347c632c75a37d382443ae379738

The state-assisted test transaction was:

0xe4cbdffa9002b0283c2c71cc19ec646b85cb58274b8f45d72496e78ae96b4cbd

Both were confirmed on CKB testnet.

More detailed evidence is in the repository:

github.com

GitHub - Ticoworld/waymark

Contribute to Ticoworld/waymark development by creating an account on GitHub.

What about recovery time?

On the real-phone run, the full baseline path took about 60 minutes.

The state-assisted path took about 30 minutes.

But I do not want to present that as “Waymark is 2x faster.”

These were not controlled performance benchmarks.

The runs included things like:

  • manual authentication;
  • automation delays;
  • peer/network conditions;
  • discovery work;
  • observation and verification;
  • restart checks.

The useful result is simpler:

the restored state avoided rebuilding some work, and the wallet still reached the same correct chain state.

A proper performance benchmark would need a different test setup.

Why I think this matters

Wallet recovery is usually discussed mostly as:

Can I recover my keys?

That is obviously the most important part.

But with a light-client wallet, there is another question:

Can I also recover the useful work my wallet had already done?

Those are different things.

The seed answers:

“Which wallet do I own?”

The saved state can help answer:

“What had this wallet already discovered and processed?”

Waymark keeps those responsibilities separate.

The seed and keys remain responsible for ownership and signing.

The saved state only helps the recovered wallet continue from previous work.

And the chain remains responsible for telling the wallet what is currently true.

One useful thing I found while testing

While checking the DAO state during this work, I also found a separate issue in Pocket’s DAO reward estimate.

The DAO reader was using 61 CKB as the occupied capacity when calculating compensation, while a DAO deposit Cell actually occupies 102 CKB.

That caused the displayed compensation estimate to be slightly too high.

It did not affect wallet ownership, principal or the actual unlock transaction path.

I reported it here:

github.com/RaheemJnr/pocket-node

fix(dao): DaoDepositReader still uses 61 CKB occupied capacity for compensation

opened 12:37PM - 06 Oct 26 UTC
closed 05:46PM - 06 Oct 26 UTC
Ticoworld

## Summary While testing a real 1,000 CKB DAO deposit on Pocket v1.8.5, I found… that `DaoDepositReader` still calculates DAO compensation using 61 CKB occupied capacity instead of 102 CKB. This appears to be a remaining reader/display issue related to the older fix in #315. The actual unlock path now uses the correct 102 CKB value, but the DAO reader still passes `61_00000000L` when calculating displayed compensation. ## Observed Testnet DAO deposit: - Principal: 1,000 CKB - Pocket cached compensation: 22,530 shannons - Canonical compensation at the same comparison point: 21,546 shannons Pocket's value is slightly higher than the canonical result. ## Root cause A standard DAO deposit Cell occupies: - 8 bytes capacity - 53 bytes lock Script - 33 bytes DAO type Script - 8 bytes data Total: 102 bytes / 102 CKB occupied capacity. Pocket already defines the correct value as: `DaoConstants.DEPOSIT_OCCUPIED_SHANNONS = 10_200_000_000L` However, `DaoDepositReader.kt` still passes: `61_00000000L` to `nativeCalculateMaxWithdraw()` in both: - active deposited-cell compensation calculation - withdrawing-cell compensation calculation This effectively treats an extra 41 CKB as compensation-bearing capacity and slightly inflates the displayed reward. ## Relation to #315 #315 previously fixed the same 61 vs 102 CKB occupied-capacity issue in the actual phase-2 unlock path. That path now uses the correct 102 CKB constant. This issue is for the remaining calculation in `DaoDepositReader`. ## Impact From the paths checked: - DAO ownership/state identity is unaffected - deposit principal is unaffected - actual unlock calculation uses the correct 102 CKB value - displayed/cached compensation is slightly too high - derived totals/APC may also be affected ## Suggested fix Replace the hardcoded `61_00000000L` values in `DaoDepositReader` with: `DaoConstants.DEPOSIT_OCCUPIED_SHANNONS` in both compensation branches. ## Acceptance - Active DAO deposit compensation matches the canonical calculation - Withdrawing DAO compensation uses 102 CKB occupied capacity - Existing unlock behavior remains unchanged

The fix was added, tested and merged into Pocket:

github.com/RaheemJnr/pocket-node

fix(dao): compensation uses the 102 CKB a deposit cell occupies, not 61 (#550) (#551)

main ← fix/550-dao-occupied-capacity
opened 05:31PM - 06 Oct 26 UTC
RaheemJnr
+419 -17

## Problem `DaoDepositReader` passed `61_00000000L` (61 CKB, the size of a plai…n secp256k1 cell) as the occupied capacity to `nativeCalculateMaxWithdraw`, for both deposited and withdrawing cells. A Nervos DAO deposit cell occupies 102 CKB (8 capacity + 53 lock + 33 type + 8 data), and the occupied part earns no compensation. The unlock transaction already used `DaoConstants.DEPOSIT_OCCUPIED_SHANNONS` (102 CKB), so only the displayed and cached compensation was wrong. Effect: every displayed compensation was inflated by `(C - 61) / (C - 102)`. The reporter's 1,000 CKB deposit showed 22,530 shannons against the canonical 21,546, which is exactly `21,546 * 939 / 898`. Principal, ownership and the unlock transaction were never affected. ## What changed - `DaoDepositReader`: both branches now go through one private `compensationFor(depositDao, endDao, capacity)` helper that passes `DaoConstants.DEPOSIT_OCCUPIED_SHANNONS`. No other place in app, shared, iOS Swift or the Rust bridge computes DAO compensation with a hardcoded occupied value (the Rust `calculate_max_withdraw` takes it as a parameter; the iOS app does not call it yet). The 61 CKB values in `SendViewModel` and `TransactionBuilder.MIN_CELL_CAPACITY` are the correct minimum secp256k1 cell size and are untouched. - Cache: live DAO cells are recomputed on every scan and written through to `dao_cells`, so they correct themselves on the next refresh. A row the live scan no longer returns (outside the sync window, or mid-unlock) was shown from its stored `compensation` and never rewritten, so a withdrawing position there would have kept the inflated figure for good. `GatewayRepository.mergeWithCachedDaoDeposits` now recomputes those rows via `DaoDepositReader.recomputeCachedCompensation`, using only the Room header cache (never waits on peers): a withdrawing row is measured to its withdraw block, a deposited row to the current tip. The corrected value is written back when it changed, through a new `DaoCellDao.updateCompensation` that sets only the `compensation` column and skips a `COMPLETED` row (matched on txHash, index, network and walletId). A whole-row upsert of the copy read earlier in the merge would race #529's retirement and bring a claimed deposit back. If a header is not cached, the stored row is shown as before. No Room migration, no schema change. - Totals: total compensation, per-deposit APC and the weighted APC in the overview and DAO screen all derive from `DaoDeposit.compensation`, so they follow without a separate change. ## Tests - New `DaoDepositReaderCompensationTest` (6 tests): the occupied capacity passed for a deposited cell and for a withdrawing cell is `DEPOSIT_OCCUPIED_SHANNONS`; cached withdrawing and deposited rows are recomputed against the right end block; a missing header or a withdrawing row without a withdraw header leaves the stored value alone. - It reuses `DaoUnlockShadowLightClientNative` (extended with `nativeGetCells`, a recorded call list for max-withdraw, and an optional transaction override) instead of a second shadow, since `LightClientNative` is a Kotlin object and Robolectric binds one shadow per sandbox. - Two new `GatewayRepositoryDaoUnlockTest` cases. In the first, a cached mid-unlock row is retired `COMPLETED` while its compensation is being recomputed, and it must stay `COMPLETED`. In the second, an outside-window row's recomputed compensation is shown and written back without changing its status. - Mutation probes: putting `61_00000000L` back makes the 4 compensation tests fail (`occupied=6100000000` vs expected `10200000000`). Putting back the whole-row `upsertDaoCell(entity.copy(...))` makes the retirement test fail (`expected:<[COMPLETED]> but was:<[UNLOCKABLE]>`). - `./gradlew test :shared:testAndroidHostTest :app:assembleDebug :app:checkNoCkbSdkOnRuntimeClasspath -x cargoBuild`: green. App unit tests go from 1113 to 1121 per variant; shared stays at 263. Fixes #550 Thanks @Ticoworld for the precise report.

That issue was separate from the Waymark recovery result, but it came out of the testing.

Current scope

Waymark is not a finished production wallet feature.

It is also not something I am claiming already works across every CKB wallet.

The current end-to-end proof is on Pocket Node.

I have not yet validated the same recovery flow on:

  • Neuron;
  • iBytes;
  • or other CKB wallets/light-client applications.

The current proof is also limited to the environment I tested:

  • one pinned Pocket version;
  • CKB testnet;
  • two accounts;
  • one active DAO deposit;
  • one real Android device;
  • and the specific saved-state format used in the experiment.

Things like cross-version migration, different wallet architectures, much larger histories, hostile/corrupt source backups and production backup UX still need separate work if this goes further.

What happens next?

For now I wanted to put the result in front of the CKB community rather than keep testing more wallets privately.

The main question I have is:

Is this recovery model useful enough to explore beyond Pocket?

For example:

  • Should something like this simply become a Pocket feature?
  • Would it be useful to test the same recovery model on another CKB wallet or light-client application?
  • If the same need appears in multiple wallets, is there a useful reusable part?
  • Or is wallet state recovery something each wallet should own independently?

I think the Pocket proof is enough to have that discussion now.

If there is interest, the next step can be decided from there instead of trying to build support for every wallet first.

Waymark:

github.com

GitHub - Ticoworld/waymark

Contribute to Ticoworld/waymark development by creating an account on GitHub.

Feedback from wallet developers, light-client developers and anyone who has dealt with wallet recovery/state reconstruction would be very useful.
